photos.description: First sighting of this bird. Enjoyed these guys hopping from spot to spot.
Spotted on top of a tree during a group walk through Propspect Park.
Spotted in Central Park, while enjoying the company of a group of other random birders.
One of my favorite birds, and a subject that always photographs well.
A little too far away for a great shot, but I just loved his scary power!
I've heard so many times that hummingbirds are very territorial, but seeing in action was amazing.
Watched a large group of these cranes circle around and then land in a marshy area, surrounded with a group of other birders and photographers.
I loved the synced up nature of the flight here.
The closest I've been to a peregrine, I just wish he was out from behind that branch.
We saw these flying over our heads on a walk to join a local birding club to do some bird tagging. I've seen them out in Seattle but never out east.
Loved the contrast here. In reality, there were dozens of these finches in this area all together.
Again too far away, but another bird I love. Surprisingly this one just sat here for a long time rather than their usual darting back and forth for bugs.
While this one only had one leg, they seemed to be doing just fine.
Took this at the Cornell bird lab, and thought the merlin at the home of Merlin was too much to pass up.
Incredible bird that you can see just on any given day.
These guys were chirping up a storm waiting for their dinner.
Unique situation here for the green heron from my experience, sitting on top of a tree where they are usually hiding in the growth.
These swallows were poking out of the houses all over the preserve.
This was amazing to see, more great blue herons than I've ever seen. Apparently thought this is too close to the power lines, and they are looking to move it.
Heard this guy clucking in the brush, and was able to finally catch a quick look.
Saw this one up in the mountains, close to a gun range of all things.
Only noticed later that this hawk has half a squirrel(?) in its talons.
You have your diving ducks and your dabbling ducks, and this is a diving dabbler.
Scene of the crime right in my own backyard.
Coldest I've ever been taking this photo, and looks like they felt the same.
Caught this guy staring at me through my window.
We were at the preserve and a ranger came up to us and said "búho" and waved us along to find this.
This was just in someone's yard along the Tigre river.
Learned that monk parakeets are basically the small pigeons of Argentina, and people feel the same about them.
Another instance of a ranger taking us to an owl, we'd have probably walked past it many times before spotting.
First waxwing spot, right outside of my mother in law's house.
Just sat here while we got a bit closer and closer to get these.
Did not expect to see these up in the trees.
Part of a falconing demonstration
Rockaway beach

American Goldfinch.about: A seed-eating finch; males turn bright yellow in summer. It nests late, timed to thistle seed.

American Kestrel.about: North America's smallest falcon, often seen hovering over fields or perched on wires; it hunts insects, rodents and small birds.

American Oystercatcher.about: A shorebird with a bright orange bill built to pry open shellfish.

American Robin.about: A familiar thrush that hunts earthworms on lawns; one of the first songs of the dawn chorus.

Bald Eagle.about: The US national bird. Adults get their white head and tail at about five years old; it feeds mostly on fish.

Baltimore Oriole.about: A flame-orange and black songbird that weaves a hanging, sock-like nest.

Barn Swallow.about: A swallow with a deeply forked tail that builds mud nests on buildings and bridges.

Belted Kingfisher.about: A shaggy-crested fish hunter with a rattling call. Unusually for birds, the female is the more colorful sex.

Black Scoter.about: An all-black sea duck (males have a knobby yellow-orange bill) that winters off Atlantic beaches.

Black-and-white Warbler.about: Creeps along trunks and branches like a nuthatch, probing bark for insects.

Black-necked Stilt.about: A black-and-white shorebird with extraordinarily long pink legs.

Bufflehead.about: A tiny diving duck; males have a big white patch on an iridescent head.

Burrowing Owl.about: A long-legged owl that lives in burrows in open grassland and is often active by day.

Canada Goose.about: A large goose with a black neck and white chinstrap, common in parks and on lawns.

Cedar Waxwing.about: A sleek, crested fruit-eater named for the waxy red tips on its wing feathers.

Checkered Woodpecker.about: A small, finely barred woodpecker of South American open woodland.

Cinnamon Teal.about: A small western duck; breeding males are a deep cinnamon-red with red eyes.

Cocoi Heron.about: The South American counterpart of the Great Blue Heron, with a black cap and a white neck.

Common Loon.about: A heavy-boned diving bird with a haunting yodel; it winters in gray plumage on coastal waters.

Common Yellowthroat.about: A skulking warbler of wet thickets; males wear a black bandit mask.

Cooper's Hawk.about: A crow-sized woodland hawk with a long, rounded tail. A frequent visitor to backyard feeders, where it hunts songbirds.

Crested Caracara.about: A long-legged falcon that behaves like a hawk-vulture hybrid, walking the ground for prey and carrion.

Dark-eyed Junco.about: A gray 'snowbird' that flashes white outer tail feathers; common in winter.

Double-collared Seedeater.about: A small seed-eating tanager; males have a black throat and a white band below it.

Double-crested Cormorant.about: A diving fish-eater often seen perched with its wings spread out to dry.

Downy Woodpecker.about: The smallest North American woodpecker and a common feeder visitor.

Eastern Phoebe.about: A tail-wagging flycatcher that calls its own name and often nests under bridges and eaves.

Eurasian Eagle-Owl.about: One of the largest owls in the world, with orange eyes and long ear tufts.

European Starling.about: Released in Central Park in 1890, it now numbers in the tens of millions across North America.

Gadwall.about: A subtly patterned gray-brown dabbling duck; it often steals food from diving ducks and coots.

Giant Wood-Rail.about: A large, loud rail of South American marshes, known for its raucous group choruses.

Gilded Hummingbird.about: Also called the Gilded Sapphire: a coppery-gold hummingbird with a red bill and golden tail.

Golden Eagle.about: A huge eagle of open country with golden nape feathers that can dive at more than 240 km/h.

Golden-billed Saltator.about: A gray songbird with a bold white eyebrow and a bright orange-yellow bill.

Gray Catbird.about: A slate-gray mimic that mews like a cat and strings together borrowed phrases.

Grayish Baywing.about: A gray-brown blackbird with rufous wings that often nests in other birds' old nests.

Great Blue Heron.about: The largest heron in North America; it stalks fish in shallow water and flies with its neck folded into an S.

Great Crested Flycatcher.about: A cavity-nesting flycatcher with a lemon belly that often weaves shed snakeskin into its nest.

Great Egret.about: A tall, all-white heron with a yellow bill and black legs. Plume hunting nearly wiped it out around 1900.

Great Horned Owl.about: A large, powerful owl with prominent ear tufts that nests earlier in the year than almost any other North American bird.

Great Kiskadee.about: A loud, bold flycatcher with a black-and-white masked head, named for its 'kis-ka-dee' call.

Greater Scaup.about: A diving duck that winters in big rafts on coastal bays; males show a rounded, green-glossed head.

Green Heron.about: A small, stocky heron that sometimes drops bait onto the water to lure fish, one of the few tool-using birds.

Harris's Hawk.about: A chocolate-and-chestnut hawk that hunts cooperatively in family groups; a favorite of falconers.

Hooded Siskin.about: A goldfinch relative of South America; males have a black hood over yellow plumage.

Horned Grebe.about: A small diving grebe; breeding adults have golden 'horns', while winter birds are crisp black and white.

House Sparrow.about: An introduced, city-loving sparrow that is closely tied to human settlements worldwide.

Killdeer.about: A plover that fakes a broken wing to lure predators away from its nest.

Lazuli Bunting.about: A western bunting; males are turquoise-blue with an orange breast and white wing bars.

Long-tailed Duck.about: A sea duck that can dive deeper than 60 m; males have long, slender tail plumes.

Magnolia Warbler.about: A yellow-and-black warbler with a distinctive tail pattern: white band near the base, black tip.

Mallard.about: The familiar ancestor of most domestic ducks; males have a glossy green head.

Maroon-bellied Parakeet.about: A green parakeet with a maroon belly patch and a long reddish tail, from Atlantic forests.

Merlin.about: A compact, powerful falcon that ambushes small birds in fast, low flight. Increasingly common in cities and towns.

Monk Parakeet.about: The only parrot that builds stick nests. Feral colonies thrive in Brooklyn as well as in its native Argentina.

Mourning Dove.about: A slender dove with a soft, mournful coo; its wings whistle on takeoff.

Muscovy Duck.about: A large tropical duck with red facial warts; widely domesticated and often feral in parks.

Mute Swan.about: A large white swan with an orange bill, introduced to North America from Europe.

Neotropic Cormorant.about: A slim, long-tailed cormorant common across Central and South America.

Northern Cardinal.about: A crested songbird; the male is brilliant red. Both sexes sing.

Northern Flicker.about: A woodpecker that often feeds on the ground, mostly on ants. Eastern birds flash yellow under the wings and tail.

Northern Harrier.about: Glides low over marshes and fields with wings in a shallow V; has an owl-like facial disk for hunting by sound.

Northern Shoveler.about: A dabbling duck with an oversized, spoon-shaped bill that it uses to strain food from the water.

Northern Waterthrush.about: A streaky warbler that walks along the edges of water, bobbing its tail.

Osprey.about: A fish-eating raptor that dives feet-first into water. Builds large stick nests on platforms, poles and channel markers.

Ovenbird.about: A ground-walking warbler named for its domed nest; it sings a loud 'teacher-teacher-teacher'.

Palm Warbler.about: A ground-feeding warbler that constantly bobs its tail; an early spring migrant.

Peregrine Falcon.about: Famous for high-speed hunting stoops; recovered from DDT-era declines and now nests on bridges and skyscrapers.

Red-bellied Woodpecker.about: A zebra-backed woodpecker with a red cap; the red belly that gives it its name is faint and hard to see.

Red-breasted Merganser.about: A fish-eating diving duck with a shaggy crest and a thin, serrated red bill.

Red-breasted Nuthatch.about: A small conifer nuthatch with a black eye stripe and a tinny 'yank-yank' call.

Red-tailed Hawk.about: The most widespread hawk in North America, often perched along highways. Adults show a brick-red tail.

Red-winged Blackbird.about: A marsh blackbird; males display red and yellow shoulder patches and sing 'conk-la-ree!'

Ring-necked Duck.about: A diving duck named for a faint chestnut neck ring that is hard to see; the white ring on its bill is easier.

Ring-necked Pheasant.about: A long-tailed game bird from Asia, introduced widely; males have a white neck ring and red face wattles.

Rock Pigeon.about: The city pigeon, descended from domesticated cliff-dwelling doves.

Rosy-billed Pochard.about: A South American diving duck; males have a bright rose-red bill with a swollen knob at the base.

Ruby-throated Hummingbird.about: The only hummingbird that breeds in the eastern US. Many cross the Gulf of Mexico nonstop on migration.

Rufous Hornero.about: The national bird of Argentina; it builds a domed mud nest shaped like a clay oven.

Rufous-bellied Thrush.about: The national bird of Brazil, a robin-like thrush with an orange belly.

Saffron Finch.about: A bright yellow, orange-crowned finch of open country; despite the name, it is a tanager.

Sandhill Crane.about: A tall gray crane with a red forehead and a rolling, bugling call. Has one of the longest fossil records of any living bird.

Savannah Sparrow.about: A streaky grassland sparrow, often with a yellow wash above the eye.

Say's Phoebe.about: A soft gray-brown flycatcher with a cinnamon belly, typical of dry open country in the West; like other phoebes, it constantly dips its tail while perched.

Shiny Cowbird.about: A glossy purple-black brood parasite that lays its eggs in other birds' nests.

Silver Teal.about: A South American dabbling duck with a blue bill, yellow at the base, and a pale cheek under a dark cap.

Snowy Egret.about: A slender white egret with a black bill and bright yellow feet that it uses to stir up prey.

Song Sparrow.about: A streaky sparrow with a central breast spot, and one of the most variable birds in North America.

Southern House Wren.about: The South American form of the House Wren, common around homes and gardens.

Southern Yellowthroat.about: A South American relative of the Common Yellowthroat; males have a black mask with a gray border.

Striated Heron.about: A small, widespread heron of the tropics, the close relative of the Green Heron.

Tree Swallow.about: An iridescent blue-green swallow that gathers in huge flocks on migration.

Tropical Screech-Owl.about: A small, common owl of Latin American woodlands and city parks, with a purring trill.

Wattled Jacana.about: Walks on floating plants on very long toes. Males incubate the eggs and raise the chicks.

White-throated Hummingbird.about: A green hummingbird with a crisp white throat, common in gardens in southeastern South America.

White-throated Sparrow.about: Sings 'Old Sam Peabody, Peabody'. It comes in white-striped and tan-striped forms.

Wilson's Warbler.about: A small yellow warbler; males wear a neat black cap.

Wood Duck.about: A strikingly patterned duck that nests in tree cavities; ducklings leap from the nest within a day of hatching.

Worm-eating Warbler.about: A plain warbler with bold head stripes that probes dead leaves for insects (not worms).

Yellow Warbler.about: An all-yellow warbler; males show chestnut streaks on the breast.

Yellow-crowned Night-Heron.about: A crab specialist of coastal marshes, with a boldly striped black-and-white face.

Yellow-headed Blackbird.about: A marsh blackbird of the West with a vivid yellow head; its song sounds like a rusty gate.
